# Description of the relationship of interest

Our data come from Eurostat and cover the period from 2014 to 2023
across European countries.

## Variable X : Inequality of income distribution (S80/S20 ratio)

The inequality of income distribution is expressed through the S80/S20
income quintile share ratio, which compares the total income received by
the 20% of the population with the highest income (the richest quintile)
to that received by the 20% with the lowest income (the poorest
quintile). This indicator is a ratio without units, meaning it is not
expressed in percentages. It provides a clear measure of how unevenly
income is distributed among individuals in a society. A lower ratio
(close to 1) indicates a more equal income distribution, while a higher
ratio reflects greater inequality, where the richest earn many times
more than the poorest. For example, a ratio of 4 means that the top 20%
of earners receive four times the income of the bottom 20%.

### Variable Y : Healthy life years

We know people are living longer. However, do we live longer and better
or do we gain only years of life in bad health?

The indicator of healthy life years (HLY) measures the number of
remaining years that a person of specific age is expected to live
without any severe or moderate health problems. The notion of health
problem for Eurostat's HLY is reflecting a disability dimension and is
based on a self-perceived question which aims to measure the extent of
any limitations, for at least six months, because of a health problem
that may have affected respondents as regards activities they usually do
(the so-called GALI - Global Activity Limitation Instrument foreseen in
the annual EU-SILC survey). The indicator is therefor also called
disability-free life expectancy (DFLE). So, HLY is a composite indicator
that combines mortality data with health status data.

HLY also monitor health as a productive or economic factor. An increase
in healthy life years is one of the main goals for European health
policy. And it would not only improve the situation of individuals but
also result in lower levels of public health care expenditure. If
healthy life years are increasing more rapidly than life expectancy, it
means that people are living more years in better health.

## Interest of studying the relationship between Inequality of income distribution and Healthy life years

Studying the relationship between income inequality and healthy life
years is important because socioeconomic factors have a major influence
on health outcomes. Higher income inequality can lead to disparities in
access to healthcare, education, nutrition, and living conditions, which
may reduce the number of years people live in good health. Understanding
this relationship helps policymakers design more effective strategies to
promote social equity and public health, ultimately improving overall
well-being and reducing health inequalities within the population.
Moreover, this type of analysis highlights the close links between
economic conditions and well-being, and it aligns fully with the logic
of sustainable development. It directly contributes to the United
Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly Goal 10
(Reduced Inequalities) and Goal 3 (Good Health and Well-being).

# Description of our data

## Measure of X

The variable X (inequality of income distribution) is measured by the
S80/S20 income quintile share ratio. This indicator compares the total
income received by the 20% of the population with the highest income to
that received by the 20% with the lowest income. The ratio is a
dimensionless number (not expressed in percentages). The data are
typically collected and published by Eurostat, based on household income
surveys conducted in each country.

## Measure of Y

The variable Y (healthy life years) is measured as the average number of
years a person can expect to live in good health, free from serious
illness or disability. It is based on two main components: life
expectancy and self-perceived health status, often gathered through
population health surveys. The indicator is expressed in years, and data
are available from Eurostat.

## The columns used to merge both datasets X and Y

The two datasets are merged using the columns as both variables are
measured annually and reported for each European country. These common
identifiers allow for an accurate match between income inequality data
and healthy life years data for the same country and year.

## The unit of observation in the final dataset

The unit of observation in the final dataset is a country-year pair.
Each row represents a specific country in a specific year (for example,
France 2019 or Germany 2021).

## The number of observation in the final dataset

The final dataset contains 330 observations, corresponding to the number
of country-year combinations available after merging both datasets.

# The goal of the project

In summary, this project aims to study the relationship between income
inequality and healthy life years across European countries over the
period 2014 to 2023. The purpose is to better understand how economic
disparities can influence health and well-being within societies.

# Descriptive statistics

## The distribution of the variable "inequality of income distribution"

```{r , echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE, comment = ""}
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    country = as.factor(country),
    year = as.numeric(year)
  )
```

## Histogram and density plot of the variable "inequality of income distribution"

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE, comment = ""}

ggplot(df, aes(x = inequality_income_dist)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 20, fill = "lightblue", color = "black",na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_density(color = "blue", linewidth = 1,na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Income Inequality",
    x = "Inequality of income distribution",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

The histogram shows a right-skewed distribution, with a main peak around
the value 4, indicating that most observations correspond to a moderate
level of income inequality. The frequency gradually decreases for higher
values, revealing the presence of a few cases of very high inequality,
but these are relatively rare. This pattern suggests that, across the
countries studied, income distribution is fairly balanced for most,
while a small number experience significant income disparities.

## Distribution of the variable "Healthy life years"

## Histogram and density plot of the variable "Healthy life years"

```{r, echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE, comment = ""}
ggplot(df, aes(x = healthy_life_years)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 20, fill = "lightblue", color = "black",na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_density(color = "blue", linewidth = 1,na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of healthy life years",
    x = "healthy life years",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

The histogram of healthy life years displays a roughly symmetrical
distribution, slightly skewed to the right, centered around 63 years.
This indicates that the majority of individuals of countries have a
moderate to high number of healthy life years, typically between 60 and
65 years, with only a few cases enjoying notably longer healthy lives
(up to 75 years). The moderate spread implies limited variation in
health outcomes, suggesting a relatively homogeneous and overall
favorable health situation.

## The average evolution of inequality_income and healthy_years in Sweden and Greece.

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE}
# Filter and compute yearly averages for the two countries
df_SG<- df %>%
  filter(country %in% c("Sweden", "Greece"))%>%
  group_by(country, year)%>%
  summarise(
    mean_x = mean(inequality_income_dist, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_y = mean (healthy_life_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Average evolution of income inequality in Sweden vs Greece

ggplot(df_SG, aes(x = year, y = mean_x, color = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Average evolution of Income Inequality in Sweden and Greece",
       x = "Year", y = " Mean inequality_income_dist",
       color = "Country") +
  theme_minimal()


```

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Average evolution of healthy life years in Sweden and Greece

ggplot(df_SG, aes(x = year, y = mean_y, color = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Average evolution of healthy life years in Sweden and Greece",
       x = "Year", y = " Average of healthy life years",
       color = "Country") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Sweden and Greece make an interesting comparison because they represent
two contrasting socio-economic models: Sweden is characterized by low
inequality income distribution and strong welfare redistribution, while
Greece has historically experienced higher inequality, notably
intensified after the 2008 financial crisis. In terms of wealth, Sweden
generally maintains high and stable accumulation, whereas Greece has
faced more volatility and losses during periods of economic instability.
Comparing these two countries therefore provides valuable insight into
how different economic structures and political strategies; strong
welfare protections versus financial vulnerability; shape the evolution
of inequality (X) and healthy life years (Y) over time.

## Ranking countries by the change in X and Y between the first and last year

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# 1. Compute the change of X and Y between first and last year for each country
df_change <- df %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(
    X_change = mean(inequality_income_dist[year == max(year)], na.rm = TRUE) -
               mean(inequality_income_dist[year == min(year)], na.rm = TRUE),
    Y_change = mean(healthy_life_years[year == max(year)], na.rm = TRUE) -
               mean(healthy_life_years[year == min(year)], na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop" # avoids the summarise grouping warning
  ) %>%
  # Remove countries with NA values
  filter(!is.na(X_change) & !is.na(Y_change))

# 2. Barplot for X change
p_X_change <- ggplot(df_change, aes(x = reorder(country, -X_change), y = X_change)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Change in inequality_income ",
       x = "Country", y = "Change in X") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = 10)),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  ) +
  coord_flip()

# 3. Barplot for Y change
p_Y_change <- ggplot(df_change, aes(x = reorder(country, -Y_change), y = Y_change)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkgreen", width = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Change in healthy_years by country",
       x = "Country", y = "Change in Y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = 10)),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  ) +
  coord_flip()

# 4. Display the two barplots side by side
p_X_change + p_Y_change
```

# Relationship between Inequality of income distribution and healthy life years

## Scatter plot for the relationship between Y and X with linear fit

In order to improve the comparability of the variables, we standardized
inequality_income_dist and healthy_life_years. Since these two
indicators are not expressed using the same unit of measurement, it was
initially difficult to clearly observe the relationship between them.
Standardization places both variables on the same scale, with a mean of
0 and a standard deviation of 1, which facilitates graphical
visualization and the interpretation of regression coefficients. From
this point onward, all analyses in this section are performed using the
standardized values of X and Y, allowing for a clearer and more
consistent examination of their relationship and the relative magnitude
of their variations.

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Let's standardized our variables 
df$inequality_income_std<- as.numeric(scale(df$inequality_income_dist, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE))
df$healthy_life_std<- as.numeric(scale(df$healthy_life_years, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE))

```

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
df_noNA<- df %>%
  filter(!is.na(inequality_income_std) & !is.na(healthy_life_std))
  
ggplot(df_noNA, aes(x = inequality_income_std, y = healthy_life_std)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "steelblue") +           # scatter points
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y~x, se = TRUE, color = "red") +   # linear regression line
  labs(title = "Scatter plot between inequality income of distribution  and healthy life years with linear fit",
       x = "inequality_income_std",
       y = "healthy_life_std") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Scatter plot for the relationship between Y and X with a quadratic fit

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ggplot(df_noNA, aes(x = inequality_income_std, y = healthy_life_std)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "steelblue") +          
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y~poly(x,2), se = TRUE, color = "red") +  
  labs(title = "Scatter plot between inequality income of distribution  and healthy life years with quadratic fit",
       x = "inequality_income_std",
       y = "healthy_life_std") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Compute within-country year-to-year changes

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
df_noNA_change<- df_noNA %>%
  arrange(country, year) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  mutate(
    dinequality_income_std = inequality_income_std - lag(inequality_income_std),
    dhealthy_life_std = healthy_life_std - lag(healthy_life_std)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter (!is.na(dinequality_income_std) & !is.na(dhealthy_life_std))
```

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Quick check
head(df_noNA_change, 5)
```

## Scatter plot between dinequality_income_std and dhealthy_life_std with linear fit

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ggplot(df_noNA_change, aes(x = dinequality_income_std, y = dhealthy_life_std))+
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "purple")+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y~x, se = TRUE, color = "black") +
  labs(title = " Scatter plot between d(inequality_income_std) and d(healthy_life_std)",
     x = " change in inequality_income (std)",
     y = "change in healthy_years (std)"
     )+
  theme_minimal()
  
```

## Regress Y on X

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
model_1 <- lm(healthy_life_std ~ inequality_income_std, data = df)
```

### Estimation table of model_1

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Table of estimation_results
kable(summary(model_1)$coefficients ,caption= "Effect of inequality_income on healthy_life")
```

## Regress Y on X controlling for country fixed effects.

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
model_2<- lm(healthy_life_std ~ inequality_income_std + factor(country) -1, 
           data = df)
```

### Estimation table of model_1 vs model_2

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Table of estimation_result
screenreg(list(model_1, model_2), stars = c(0.1, 0.05, 0.01))
```

## Regress Y on X controlling for year and country fixed effects.

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
model_3<- lm(healthy_life_std ~ inequality_income_std + factor(year)
                          + factor(country) -1, data = df)  
```

### Estimation table of model_1 vs model_2 vs model_3

```{r, comment = "", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
screenreg(list(model_1, model_2, model_3), stars = c(0.1, 0.05, 0.01))
```

## Interpretation

The estimated coefficients show a consistently negative relationship
between income inequality and healthy life expectancy. In the simple
model, the coefficient is β = -0.11, indicating that an increase of one
standard deviation in inequality is associated with a 0.11
standard-deviation decrease in years of healthy life. When country fixed
effects are added, the effect becomes stronger (β = -0.19) and more
statistically significant. This means that when comparing a country to
itself over time thereby controlling for structural differences across
countries such as development level, healthcare systems, or cultural
factors an increase in inequality is associated with a more pronounced
loss of healthy life years. In the model that also includes year fixed
effects, the coefficient remains negative (β = -0.16) and significant,
confirming the robustness of the relationship even after accounting for
time specific shocks, such as the pandemic or economic fluctuations. The
coefficients associated with the country and year fixed effects
reinforce this interpretation. The country fixed effects show that some
countries have, on average, higher healthy life expectancy (positive
coefficients, for example, Sweden, Iceland, Malta), while others remain
consistently below the baseline (negative coefficients, for example,
Bulgaria, Latvia, Slovakia). Finally, the year fixed effects are mostly
negative, indicating an overall decline in healthy life years during the
study period, regardless of inequality levels. Taken together, these
results show not only that income inequality has a direct, statistically
significant, and relatively stable effect on health, but also that this
effect persists even after controlling for major structural and temporal
factors.

## Policy implications for economic decision-making

The estimates show that income inequality has a negative, significant,
and robust effect on healthy life expectancy. These results suggest that
public policies specifically targeting the reduction of income
disparities could serve as a key lever for improving population health.
First, more progressive redistributive policies (tax reforms, increased
progressiveness of income taxes, tax credits for low income households)
would help reduce the inequality measured in the models and, according
to the estimated coefficients, mitigate part of the decline in healthy
life years. Second, strengthening social transfers particularly through
housing benefits, targeted support for vulnerable families, or
guaranteed minimum income schemes would directly reduce economic
insecurity, a factor often associated with limited access to prevention
and healthcare.

At the same time, the country fixed effects show that structural health
differences between states are substantial. This supports the need for
policies aimed at reducing inequalities in access to health services,
notably through greater investment in primary care, prevention, mental
health, and hospital infrastructure in regions with weaker health
outcomes. Similarly, since the year fixed effects reveal a general
downward trend in health over recent years, it is crucial to implement
broad strategies that strengthen health resilience: post pandemic public
health policies, programs to combat chronic diseases, measures to reduce
work related and social stress, and initiatives that improve
environmental quality and living conditions. Finally, since an increase
of one standard deviation in inequality reduces health by about 0.16
standard deviations in the most comprehensive models, a broad economic
policy strategy aimed at reducing inequalities combining taxation,
employment, education, and health could generate significant and lasting
improvements in healthy life expectancy.
